newsitem.title: FRANCE: TWA jetliner downed by US missile, Salinger says.
newsitem.headline: TWA jetliner downed by US missile, Salinger says.

text.p: Former White House adviser Pierre Salinger on Friday cast aside U.S. denials and stood by his charge that a U.S. Navy missile accidentally shot down a TWA jumbo jet which crashed off New York in July.

Salinger said he had been given a document in Paris by an agent of the U.S. Secret Service which said the airliner, flying too low and behind schedule, had entered an area where the U.S. Navy was staging missile tests.
"The airliner was not the target of an attack...It was shot down by a military missile during a test," Salinger said.
"The paper that I have read is very, very strong proof that a missile did have a part in bringing the plane down," he told Reuters television.
A missile, a bomb or a mechanical fault have been suggested as causes for the crash of the Boeing 747 off Long Island on July 17, days before the opening of the Atlanta Olympics.
All 230 people aboard were killed. There has been no official verdict in the probe.
The FBI, the Pentagon and the Navy denied on Thursday that a missile was involved. The National Transportation Safety Board has rejected similar suggestions in the past.

Salinger, who initially made his allegations to airline officials attending a meeting in the French Mediterranean resort of Cannes, told reporters he was not surprised by the denials and offered to show the FBI his three-month-old document, which he said he had been given five weeks ago.
He suggested the evidence in his possession may have been withheld to avoid embarrassing President Bill Clinton before Tuesday's presidential election.
"Now it will be interesting to see since the election is three days ago whether there will be a change in the way they are doing the investigation," he told Reuters.
Salinger said the document showed that the Navy had conducted the test at an altitude of 13,000 feet in the belief that all aircraft in the area were flying at 21,000 feet.
The military was unaware that TWA flight 800 had taken off late from New York because of heavy traffic and was flying lower than expected to stay clear of another aircraft, he said.
The airport control tower, in "a tragic error," failed to inform the Navy, Salinger said.
"There is a lot of proof for the document. I have since talked to several individuals who have upheld what the agent said," he said. "The truth must come out."

FBI spokesman Joe Valiquette said in New York, "We are not familiar with what Mr Salinger has said...Our investigation so far has not revealed any evidence that a so-called friendly fire situation brought down TWA flight 800."
Salinger produced a picture said to have been taken at a party on Long Island at the time of the crash and purportedly showing a missile-like object streaking through the sky.
The picture was published recently by the French weekly Paris Match.
Salinger, 71, was press spokesman for the late president John F. Kennedy and later Paris bureau chief for the U.S. television network ABC.
He said he had passed on his information to an unspecified U.S. TV network which did not broadcast it. He accused the U.S. government of clamping a news blackout on the crash.

In Paris, a lawyer for the relatives of the 45 French citizens killed on board the Paris-bound airliner said he asked investigating magistrate Chantal Perdrix to question Salinger and have the Paris Match picture scrutinised by police experts.
"I think Pierre Salinger's statement should not be taken lightly," lawyer Gilles-Jean Portejoie told Reuters.
Perdrix has opened a probe into the crash to determine whether manslaughter or murder charges are warranted.
Investigators are still dredging the seabed off Long Island for evidence to explain the crash. They have established that a fuel tank exploded but not what set off the blast.
